solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: School's dealt with each boy in a busy period

indicators.note: dealt with here works as a joining phrase: the school's piece is dealt along with the next pieces in turn

parts.note: a high school is often called simply 'the High', so the school's gives High's
a boy is a son

explanation.surface: A headteacher boasts that the school has looked after every boy during a hectic stretch.
explanation.walkthrough: HIGHS comes from 'the High', the usual short name for a high school, plus the possessive S.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourism's peak months, when hotels and resorts are fullest, are its busiest time of year.

clue.text: Form of cold storage that was designed by 16

indicators.note: a form of something is a new shape, so the letters of cold storage are reshaped

explanation.surface: A building for keeping things chilled, drawn up by the architect at 16 across.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 across is Sir Edwin Lutyens, who designed this granite house on Dartmoor in Devon, England, built between 1911 and 1930.
explanation.definitionFit: Lutyens drew up the plans for this country house, the last castle built in England, so it fits a building he designed.

clue.text: Deer going over mass of leaves in Surrey village

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece goes over, so above, the second

parts.note: a hind is a female deer
a head is a compact mass of leaves, as in a head of lettuce

explanation.surface: A deer clambers across a heap of fallen leaves near a Surrey village.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south-west of London; this village sits by the Devil's Punch Bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindhead is a village in the county of Surrey, in south-east England.

clue.text: Problem making leader of society go on and on

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here taken from society

parts.note: to nag is to go on and on, complaining repeatedly

explanation.surface: A difficulty arises when a society's chairman keeps droning on.
explanation.definitionFit: A snag is an unexpected hitch or obstacle, a kind of difficulty.

clue.text: It could be sunnier, pal, in Spain and Portugal?

indicators.note: it could be suggests the letters may form something else once rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tells a friend that Iberia might be the sunnier holiday option.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain and Portugal make up the Iberian peninsula, so what happens there is peninsular, as in the Peninsular War.

clue.text: Business qualification in wood preserve!

indicators.note: in places the qualification inside the tree's name

parts.note: elm is a wood, the timber of the elm tree
an MBA is a Master of Business Administration degree

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at the idea of keeping a business degree inside a wooden case.
explanation.definitionFit: To embalm a body is to preserve it from decay with chemicals.

clue.text: The community we've left to become vociferous — upsetting conversation

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting turns the pieces upside down, so they are read from the bottom up

parts.note: the European Union, once the European Community, which Britain left
to go can mean to become, as in go mad
vociferous means loud

explanation.surface: A grumble about Brexit: leaving the European club has made people noisy and conversation upsetting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' turns EUGOLOUD upside down. 'The community we've left' is a British view of the EU after Brexit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialogue between just two people, especially on stage, is a form of conversation.

clue.text: House in home counties or Oxford?

indicators.note: in places the house abbreviation inside the region's letters

parts.note: the home counties around London lie in the South-East, SE

explanation.surface: Is this house in the counties around London, or in the university city of Oxford?
explanation.walkthrough: The home counties are the counties surrounding London. 'Oxford' looks like the city but is a type of laced shoe, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxford is a style of lace-up leather footwear, so it is one example of the answer.

clue.text: It is the man I outrival going mad

indicators.note: going mad says the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A rival boasts of driving the other fellow crazy by outdoing him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' looks like a pronoun but is short for Italian vermouth, as in the drink gin and it.
explanation.definitionFit: In bar slang 'it' is short for the sweet Italian fortified wine, as in a gin and it.

clue.text: Very unpopular letters that editor receives

indicators.note: letters says the answer is a run of letters taken from the words that follow
receives says the phrase that editor holds the answer within it

explanation.surface: An editor gets a pile of mail from readers who loathe the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone loathed by everyone is thoroughly disliked, so very unpopular.

clue.text: Painting is first bit of art to be protected by metal bars

indicators.note: to be protected by puts the following pieces inside the metal bars

parts.note: a grille is a grating of metal bars

indicators.note: the first bit of art is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A gallery puts a precious painting behind security bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Grisaille is a style of painting done entirely in shades of grey, often imitating sculpture.

clue.text: Refreshments? Team seems not to want 'em

parts.note: a cricket or football team is an eleven

indicators.note: not to want them means the letters em are left out of seems

parts.note: 'em is the clipped form of them, written as the letters em

explanation.surface: Offered tea and biscuits, the players seem to turn them down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to want' drops EM from SEEMS, leaving SES.
explanation.definitionFit: A British mid-morning snack, usually tea and biscuits, taken around eleven o'clock.

clue.text: Pianist isn't sane, playing aboard ship

indicators.note: aboard puts the pieces on board, inside the ship's letters

parts.note: SS is the usual abbreviation for steamship
ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of sane are performed in a new order

explanation.surface: A pianist on a cruise ship is performing so wildly he seems mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges SANE into SAEN. 'isn't' looks like part of the anagram but gives AIN'T.
explanation.definitionFit: The French composer Camille Saint-Saëns was also a celebrated virtuoso pianist and organist.

clue.text: Study before exam as idiot at Oxford?

parts.note: a mug is a gullible fool
being up means being in residence at university, such as Oxford

explanation.surface: A student wonders whether cramming makes him a fool at Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug up is British slang for cramming, learning a subject quickly just before a test.

clue.text: Old-fashioned daughter, maiden maybe getting ignored

parts.note: passé means out of date, old-fashioned
a maiden is one kind of over in cricket, one with no runs scored

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned girl, a maiden perhaps, finds herself overlooked by suitors.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls; a maiden is an over from which no runs are scored.
explanation.definitionFit: To be passed over is to be overlooked, as when someone is not chosen for promotion.

clue.text: Architect configuring truly new insides

indicators.note: configuring means arranging parts into a new layout, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An architect redesigns the interior of a building to make it genuinely new.
explanation.definitionFit: Lutyens was the British architect behind New Delhi's government buildings and the Cenotaph in London.

clue.text: Poor Indra somehow having nothing to release — not even this?

indicators.note: somehow says the letters are rearranged in some way
to release means letting go of a piece, which is taken out of the pool of letters

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Indra, the Hindu god of rain, is so poor he has no water to let fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The word after Indra signals the anagram of POORINDRA, less the O that 'to release' lets go. In a drought not a drop of rain falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry weather means not one drop of rain falls, so the answer is what is missing in 'not even' a single one.

clue.text: Gloomy second person's keeping below

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: thy is the old second-person possessive, your
under means below

explanation.surface: Someone feeling low holds a second person beneath them.
explanation.definitionFit: Thundery weather is dark and overcast with storm clouds, so gloomy.

clue.text: A —–? Irritates when heard!

parts.note: the blank after A needs a word so that the two words spoken together sound like a verb meaning irritates

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank riddle about something irritating to listen to.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a' plus the missing word and it sounds like ANNOYS, which means irritates; the missing word is also a din that irritates when heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A din or racket is something that grates on the ear, irritating whoever has to listen to it.

clue.text: Terrible avenger not against showing anger

indicators.note: terrible suggests the letters are in a terrible mess, so rearranged
not says a letter is excluded from the pool before rearranging

parts.note: V, short for versus, means against

explanation.surface: A dreadful avenger, not opposed to anything, displays fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' rearranges AVENGER less the V that 'not' excludes.
explanation.definitionFit: To anger someone, used as a verb, is to make them furious, which is to infuriate them.

clue.text: Our quiet's disturbed, making us sort of blue

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown out of order, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Having our peace interrupted leaves us feeling a little blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' looks like sad, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Turquoise is a greenish-blue shade named after the gemstone.

clue.text: First person keen to go on a river that is shown on maps

indicators.note: to go on means one piece is followed by the others in sequence

parts.note: I is the first person pronoun
to keen is to wail in grief, to sob

explanation.surface: The first person eager to head out on a river that appears on the map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keen' looks like eager, but it is the verb to wail.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather charts draw lines joining places of equal atmospheric pressure, so these lines appear on maps.

clue.text: Working for a labourer is not straightforward

parts.note: working for someone is working under them
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: Employing a casual labourer is a bit shady.
explanation.definitionFit: Underhand dealings are sly and secret, the opposite of honest and direct.

clue.text: Two islands — holy person is buried beneath superior one

indicators.note: in a down clue being buried beneath means the piece sits below the others

parts.note: U stands for upper class, superior
I is the Roman numeral one
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A saint is laid to rest under a monument on a remote isle.
explanation.walkthrough: U meaning upper class, so socially superior, is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: North Uist and South Uist are a pair of islands in Scotland's Outer Hebrides, linked by causeways.

clue.text: Bargain is perfect? I missed out

indicators.note: missed out says a letter is left out of the word for perfect

parts.note: ideal means perfect

explanation.surface: A shopper wonders if a bargain is perfect after missing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A deal is an agreement or a good buy, the same as a bargain.

clue.text: See 2
One's expecting to be in this match maybe?

definitions.text: One's expecting to be in this match maybe?

parts.words: One's expecting to be in this match maybe?
parts.note: a woman who is expecting, pregnant, may be hurried into a wedding forced on the couple

explanation.surface: Someone anticipates being picked for a sporting fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expecting' suggests anticipation and 'match' a game; read instead as pregnant and a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding hurried along because the bride is pregnant, traditionally forced by her father.
